questions.learningObjective: State what the threshold frequency establishes.
questions.stem: A city memo proposes using ultraviolet lamps to clean a solar panel. The panel's coating has a threshold frequency of 9.0e14 hertz. What does that number fix?

options.text: It fixes the lowest photon frequency that can eject electrons from the coating.
It fixes the highest frequency the coating will reflect instead of absorbing.
options.misconception: confuses a threshold with a reflection cutoff

options.text: It fixes the frequency at which the emitted electron current saturates.
options.misconception: confuses the threshold with a saturation frequency

options.text: It fixes the frequency of the light the panel emits as it glows.
options.misconception: treats the threshold as an emission line

questions.explanation: The threshold frequency is the point where the photon energy h f equals the work function of the coating. Below it no photon carries enough energy to free an electron, so raising the intensity alone changes nothing.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain the evidence for matter waves.
questions.stem: A city memo asks why a beam of electrons can produce the same kind of fringe pattern as a beam of light, given that the electrons are charged particles. Write the explanation the memo requires.

answer.exemplar: Electrons are quantum objects whose motion can be described by a wavefunction, and that wavefunction spreads through a slit just as light does. Interference between the two paths a single electron could take produces the fringes, which accumulate into a pattern after many electrons arrive. The de Broglie wavelength h over p sets the fringe spacing, so electrons with the right momentum behave exactly like waves of that wavelength.

questions.explanation: Matter waves are confirmed by electron diffraction, so the interference is a property of quantum amplitudes rather than of any classical wave medium. A single electron interferes with itself across the two slits.
questions.hint: Discuss amplitudes, not classical ripples.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain the evidence for matter waves.
questions.stem: Write an account of the experimental evidence that electrons behave as waves, naming the observable that proves it and why it matters for the memo.

answer.exemplar: Electrons scattered from a crystal surface produce diffraction peaks whose angles obey the Bragg condition, exactly as a wave reflected from a lattice of planes must. Since the crystal spacing is known, the measured angles give the electron wavelength, and it agrees with the value h over p from the de Broglie relation. The fact that a single electron builds up the same interference pattern as light shows the wave character belongs to the electron itself.

questions.explanation: Electron diffraction by crystals and interference at electron double slits both produce the fringe patterns characteristic of waves. The measured wavelengths match the de Broglie prediction, which makes the evidence decisive.
questions.hint: Name the experiment and the observed fringes.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the evidence for matter waves.
questions.stem: Explain why electrons can be diffracted by a crystal even though they are charged particles with a definite trajectory.

answer.exemplar: An electron is described by a quantum amplitude that spreads out as it travels, and a crystal offers many regularly spaced planes from which the electron can scatter, so the scattered amplitudes interfere and reinforce only at particular angles. Those angles satisfy the Bragg condition, which ties them to the spacing of the atomic planes. The regular crystal therefore acts as a diffraction grating for the electron wave, and the observed angles give the de Broglie wavelength directly.

questions.explanation: A crystal plane arrangement acts as a three-dimensional diffraction grating for the electron wavefunction, so the scattered amplitudes interfere and give sharp peaks. These peaks reveal the de Broglie wavelength, not a classical trajectory.
questions.hint: Mention interference between scattered amplitudes.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the evidence for matter waves.
questions.stem: Describe how an electron double-slit experiment differs from sending classical particles through the same slits.

answer.exemplar: Sending classical particles through two slits gives two overlapping bands of impact spots, with roughly equal numbers on each side. Electrons sent one at a time give individual spots that are initially random, yet the accumulated distribution shows interference fringes of the kind light produces. The individual electron must therefore be described by an amplitude that passes through both slits and interferes with itself, so the pattern is a property of the quantum description rather than of a stream of tiny particles.

questions.explanation: The quantum prediction is a probability distribution built from interfering amplitudes, not from a sum of classical trajectories. Single-electron build-up is what rules out a simple classical explanation.
questions.hint: Contrast trajectories with amplitudes.

questions.stem: Explain why the work function of a metal is usually measured using the photoelectric effect rather than by heating the sample.

answer.exemplar: Heating a sample drives electrons out thermally, but the energy taken to release an electron then depends on the temperature, the surface conditions and the escape path, so the binding energy cannot be read off cleanly. In the photoelectric effect the energy delivered is set precisely by the photon frequency, so plotting the stopping potential against frequency gives a straight line whose intercept is the work function. The measurement is therefore direct and independent of how the electrons leave the material.

questions.explanation: Photoelectric measurements deliver a known photon energy directly, so the barrier appears as the intercept of a stopping potential against frequency plot. Thermal emission mixes in temperature and surface effects.
questions.hint: Contrast a controlled photon energy with heating.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the Compton wavelength shift.
questions.stem: Explain the physical meaning of the Compton wavelength, including why it is a property of the electron rather than of the photon.

answer.exemplar: The Compton wavelength equals the Planck constant divided by the electron's rest mass times the speed of light, and it sets the scale on which a photon transfers energy to an electron. It contains no photon quantity at all, only h, the electron mass and c, which is why every free-electron scattering process shows the same characteristic shift. Doubling the photon energy changes the size of the energy transfer but leaves this length scale untouched, so the effect reveals particle-like behaviour of light.

questions.explanation: The Compton wavelength is built from the Planck constant, the electron mass and the speed of light, so it is a property of the scattering partner. The shift it measures is independent of the incident photon energy.
questions.hint: Look at which quantities define the scale.
